content: In 1998, secretin, a gastrointestinal hormone, was proposed as a potential treatment for autism spectrum disorders (ASD) based on anecdotal evidence. This review aimed to evaluate whether intravenous secretin improves the core symptoms of ASD, other behavioral or functional aspects such as self-injurious behavior, or the quality of life for individuals with ASD and their caregivers. Additionally, the review assessed whether secretin causes any harm. This is an updated version of a review originally published in 2005. The search for relevant studies included databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, and ERIC, covering publications from 1998 (when secretin was first proposed as a treatment for ASD) to January 2010. Reference lists of trials and reviews were also examined, and experts and researchers were contacted to identify unpublished studies. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing intravenous secretin to placebo in children or adults diagnosed with ASD, provided that at least one standardized outcome measure was reported. Sixteen studies met the inclusion criteria. However, for two of these studies conducted by Repligen, only multisite data from press releases were available. The remaining 14 trials provided continuous outcome data. For trials with cross-over designs, only data from the first treatment phase were analyzed. When available, mean changes from baseline were used for meta-analyses or forest plots instead of post-treatment scores. Meta-analysis was only feasible for one outcome measure, the Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS). There was insufficient data to perform sensitivity or subgroup analyses to evaluate the impact of study quality, clinical differences in the intervention, or differences between groups, such as age or the presence of gastrointestinal symptoms. Over 900 children participated in the secretin trials. Twenty-five standardized outcome measures were used to assess core features of ASD, communication, behavior, visuospatial skills, affect, and adverse events. Additionally, one standardized measure of global impression was employed. No more than four studies used the same outcome measure in a comparable manner. When the duration from the start of the intervention to outcome assessment was reported, it ranged from three to six weeks. Although meta-analysis was not possible for most outcomes, the findings across RCTs consistently showed that secretin did not improve the core features of ASD. The authors concluded that there is no evidence to support the effectiveness of single or multiple doses of intravenous secretin as a treatment for ASD. Therefore, secretin should not currently be recommended or administered for this purpose. Further experimental research on secretin's effectiveness for ASD would only be justified if new, high-quality, and replicated scientific evidence emerges. Such evidence would need to demonstrate either a role for secretin in neurotransmission that could benefit all children with ASD or identify specific subgroups of children with ASD who might benefit due to a proven link between secretin's action and the underlying cause of their ASD or the specific challenges they face.
